newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE - Singaporeans jam gold shops after price tumble.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Singaporeans jam gold shops after price tumble.

text.p: Squinting in the bright light, a Chinese-Singaporean in singlet and shorts weighs an oversized gold bracelet in his calloused hands.
He mutters something unintelligible to a companion before handing the bracelet back and hunching over the counter to inspect more of the glinting jewellery.
Dozens of other people jostle for space in the jewellery shop at the Tiong Bahru mall to look at bracelets, rings, and rows of pendants sporting images of icons from Jesus Christ to Mickey Mouse.
"It's like lunchtime at McDonald's," one mother said before going in and buying a 22-carat gold bracelet for her daughter.

Ho Nai Chuen, managing director of the On Cheong Co jewellery store, said goldsmiths in Singapore had to work 18 or 19 hours a day for weeks to satisfy the explosive demand for necklaces, bracelets, rings and pendants.
"On weekends, you can see the flow was non-stop," Ho told Reuters. "You can see that people were rushing to buy for fear that the gold price may shoot up quite suddenly."
BOOM IN GOLD SALES BRINGS CHEER TO JEWELLERS
The Singapore buying spree was spurred by July's sharp fall in the price of gold to 12-year lows of around US$314 an ounce.
Industry analysts said a big gold jewellery shop would easily ring up sales of 400 to 500 pieces of jewellery in one weekend at the height of the buying.
Even a small shop, Ho says, can sell an average of 100 items. There are an estimated 700 gold jewellery shops in Singapore, for a population of around three million.
The World Gold Council said Singapore's consumption reached eight tonnes in the first quarter of 1997, up strongly when compared to consumption of 20 tonnes in the whole of 1996.
The big gold shops were probably grossing 100,000 Singapore dollars ($67,700) a day during weekends, while smaller outfits were posting daily sales of S$10,000, analysts said.
Ho said the most popular type of gold jewellery was the one Singaporeans call "916 gold".
The number is shorthand for jewellery, the content of which is 91.6 percent. In the West, it is known as 22-carat gold.

"They prefer the gold colour to be a bit brownish. If it is 24 carat, the colour can be too yellowish and also at the same time it's a bit soft," Ho said. "I think 70-80 percent of Singaporeans prefer gold in 22 carat."

Demand was so strong that several big jewellery stores in Singapore were forced to farm out jobs to goldsmiths in Thailand, in Penang in Malaysia and even China to meet the orders, one industry analyst said.
TRIGGER FOR PRICE FALL
The trigger for the fall in the gold price was the decision of the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) to sell 167 tonnes, or two-thirds of its reserves.

After hovering near the $340 an ounce level for several weeks, a frenzied sell-off swept gold to 12-year lows. Its price has since recovered and climbed to nearly $330 in early August before dropping again to range recently between $315 and $322 per ounce.
The gold-buying spree in Singapore's shops should slow down during the Hungry Ghost festival observed by the Chinese for most of August.
The festival is usually regarded by Chinese as an inauspicious time to make major investments such as buying large quantities of gold jewellery.
But World Gold Council Albert Cheng questioned that view.
"It is quite ironic that this kind of traditional Chinese belief is more observed outside China than in China or in Hong Kong," he said. "Younger people are trying to break away from this."
He does not believe gold buying in Singapore will slow down drastically in August and said other factors, such as "price, design, the shopping environment", were more important for buyers.
"I think the price is attractive for people who like to buy a piece of gold jewellery," he said.
Dealers predicted renewed bouts of buying if gold approached the major psychological support level of $300.
A slew of holidays in the last quarter of the year means demand is also likely to pick up strongly then.

Indians will be buying heavily ahead of the Diwali holiday at the end of October. Buying will also be strong during the Christmas season and will then peak ahead of the Chinese Lunar New Year festivities in January.
Ho said the biggest buyers of gold are middle-aged people, whose formidable purchasing power is at its peak.
"Forty-five years and above are the strong buyers," he said. "Chinese and Asian people still believe that gold is a safeguard for their assets."
The love of gold will not diminish any time soon, especially since it can always be pawned or melted down for re-sale during times of hardship, he said.
"How many commodities in the market can you buy, after (keeping) a number of years, that can still fetch a certain amount of value? Gold is the only such item," Ho declared.
"Gold is something that cannot be diminished." ($ = 1.475 Singapore Dollars)
